title: Elbert County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Elbert County wells have a 341-foot median depth. Compare yields, water levels and finished-well costs of about $23,000-$35,900 before buying land.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Elbert County
intro_html:
A well budget near Elizabeth or Kiowa should start with nearby completion records, not a countywide average alone. Elbert County's recorded median well depth is 341 feet, with a median reported pump yield of 12.0 gpm. Those are useful starting points, but the aquifer beneath the property matters more than the mailing address.

Colorado DWR records include 17,502 permitted wells countywide, with 10,074 recorded as constructed. A permit on the map is not proof that a working well exists on the ground.

sections.heading: From Ponderosa Park to Matheson, Depth Follows the Aquifer
sections.html:
Of the 10,532 wells reporting depth, the median is 341 feet and the middle half fall between 225 and 450 feet. For a drilling bid, that means the median is a planning allowance—not a depth the contractor can promise. The 90th-percentile depth is 615 feet, so deeper work is a real possibility.

Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 97% of the records. Upper Dawson and Denver are prominent named aquifers, and the cost model assumes sedimentary bedrock. Ask which aquifer the proposed well will target. Compare completed wells near Ponderosa Park, Elizabeth, Simla or Matheson in that same aquifer rather than treating every county well as a comparable.

sections.heading: What Elbert County's Reported Yields Mean for a Household
sections.html:
The 7,456 records with pump yields show a median of 12.0 gpm, with the middle half between 10.0 and 14.0 gpm. That is an encouraging household supply benchmark, provided the well can sustain it. A reported pumping rate is not the same as a long-duration test of dependable production.

The yield summary places 5% in the 1-5 gpm range and reports 0% below 1 gpm. Do not read that as a guarantee against a weak well; the summary covers reported yields, not every permit. Before buying, have the well's sustained output, recovery and pressure equipment evaluated. Also verify permitted uses before assuming household water can serve livestock or irrigation.

sections.heading: Water Levels Are Deeper Than Early Records, but Not Steadily Falling
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water, not the bottom of the drilled hole. Among 1,029 reporting wells, the median is 165 feet below ground, with the middle half at 97-240 feet. That distinction matters when evaluating pump placement and the water available above the pump during use.

Decade medians deepen from 30 feet in the 1950s to 222 feet in the 1990s, then fluctuate: 197 in the 2000s, 160 in the 2010s and 185 in the 2020s. The series suggests deeper water than in early records, but not a steady countywide decline. These are different groups of measurements, not repeated monitoring of the same wells.

sections.heading: Elbert County's Drilling Record Runs Through 2026
sections.html:
Permit issuance was highest in the supplied decade totals during the 1990s, with 4,138 permits, followed by 3,479 in the 2000s. The records show 2,240 in the 2010s and 1,404 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2026. The current decade is incomplete, and issuance does not establish when construction actually happened.

The most active drillers listed are Hamacher Well Works Inc with 3,994 records, Parker Drilling/Pump Service Inc. with 1,395, and Hier Drilling Co Inc with 1,163. Those counts show historical involvement, not current availability. When requesting a bid, ask about recent work near your property and experience with the proposed aquifer.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Well Near Elizabeth, Kiowa or Elbert
sections.html:
The supplied drilling model uses $50-$70 per foot for Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the county's 341-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $17,000-$23,900. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $23,000-$35,900.

Use that range to screen a project budget, not as a parcel-specific quote. A deeper aquifer target, difficult equipment access or a long utility route can change the scope. Have bids spell out casing, grout, pump equipment and connection work. On land near Elizabeth, Kiowa or Elbert, settle the likely house location and access route before comparing finished-well proposals.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Site Constraints Before Closing
sections.html:
The supplied environmental mapping identifies 40 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 5 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 1 historic mine feature within about 10 miles. These are screening flags, not evidence that a particular Elbert County well is contaminated. Check the actual site locations and available findings before deciding what testing the property needs.

For an existing well, arrange laboratory testing rather than judging safety by taste or clarity. Have casing and wellhead condition checked, along with septic placement and drainage around the well. For undeveloped land, discuss low-production or unsuccessful drilling terms with the driller before work starts. Keep the well, septic area, driveway and building footprint coordinated.

sections.heading: Buying Elbert County Land: Verify the Well Before the House Plan
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit, construction report and pump record. Confirm that an existing well belongs to the property and that its authorized uses match your plans. A household-use authorization should not be assumed to allow lawn irrigation or stock watering. Ask DWR what permit and water-right requirements apply before committing to a new well.

Then compare nearby completed wells around your actual location—Elizabeth, Kiowa, Elbert, Simla or Matheson—not just the county median. Match aquifer names where available. Make the purchase decision with a water-quality report, a production assessment and a site layout that leaves workable room for drilling access, septic approval and the proposed home.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Elbert County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 341 feet, and the middle half of wells are 225-450 feet deep. The 90th-percentile depth is 615 feet. These figures come from 10,532 depth reports. For a specific lot, compare nearby completed wells targeting the same aquifer before using the county median in a drilling budget.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Elbert County?
faq.a: The supplied model estimates $50-$70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 341-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $17,000-$23,900. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $23,000-$35,900. Get a written scope based on the aquifer target, access and proposed utility route.

faq.q: Do Elbert County wells produce enough water for a house?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 12.0 gpm, with the middle half at 10.0-14.0 gpm. That is a useful household benchmark, but an individual well needs testing. The records place 5% in the 1-5 gpm range. Check sustained production, recovery and permitted uses rather than relying only on the recorded pump rate.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Elbert County?
faq.a: County depth and yield records cannot establish drinking-water safety. The supplied mapping includes 40 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 5 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but proximity does not prove contamination at a well. Obtain laboratory testing and review nearby site findings, wellhead condition and septic placement before relying on the supply.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Elbert County?
faq.a: The decade medians show deeper static water levels than early records, but not a continuous decline. Median depth to water was 222 feet in the 1990s, 160 feet in the 2010s and 185 feet in the 2020s. Because these are grouped measurements from different wells, they do not establish the trend at a particular property.
